title: One hook, three letters: ج ح خ

bigIdea.text: Three letters share one hooked body. The dot decides: dot below = ج (jim), no dot = ح (ḥa), dot above = خ (kha).

proper.text: Standing alone, all three have a hook on top and a round tail below the line. ج keeps its dot inside the curve, ح has no dot, خ has one dot above. At the start or in the middle of a word only the hook is left, so look for the dot.
Sounds: ج is a firm 'j' as in 'jam'. ح is a strong, smooth breath squeezed in the middle of the throat, with no scrape. خ is like 'ch' in Scottish 'loch': a light scrape near the top of the throat.

Sifat (letter qualities): ج is 'strong' (shiddah: its sound is held back fully) and one of the five bouncing letters (qalqalah), so with a sukun it bounces. ح and خ are 'whispered' (hams: the breath keeps flowing).

provenance.title: صفة حرف (العربية) (Sifat of Arabic letters) — Arabic Wikipedia

proper.text: Heavy or light: خ is one of the seven heavy letters (خ ص ض غ ط ق ظ). ج and ح are light.

Common mistakes. English speakers: ح comes out as a plain 'h', and خ as 'k'. Persian/Urdu readers: ح is said like ه; squeeze the middle of the throat for ح. Everyone: keep ج firm, not 'zh' (as in 'measure') and not 'g'.

points.detail: Middle of the tongue (shared with ش and ي)
Middle of the throat (shared with ع)
Part of the throat nearest the mouth (shared with غ)

memoryHook.text: Dot below = j, no dot = ḥ, dot above = kh.

extras.text: In everyday Arabic, ج changes by region: 'j' in many places, 'zh' in much of North-West Africa, and 'g' in Egypt.
ح and خ are both whispered, but only خ is heavy. That is why خ sounds fuller and deeper.

tip.text: ح: smooth breath from the middle of the throat, no scrape, light. خ: higher, near the mouth, with a light scrape, heavy.

questions.q: Which letter has one dot ABOVE the hook?
explain: Right: one dot above the hook is kha.
jim's dot is below the hook (inside the curve when it stands alone).
ḥa has no dot at all.
dhal also has one dot above, but its body is a small angle, not a hook.

options: The deepest part of the throat, nearest the chest
The part of the throat nearest the mouth
explain: Right: ḥa (with ʿayn) comes from the middle of the throat.
That is the place of hamza and ha (ه).
That is the place of jim, shin and ya.
That is the place of kha and ghayn.

questions.q: Which letter of this family is heavy?
explain: Right: kha is one of the seven heavy letters.
ḥa is light.
jim is light.
Only kha is heavy; jim and ḥa are light.

questions.q: Which letter of this family bounces (qalqalah) when it has a sukun?
explain: Right: jim is one of the five qalqalah letters (ق ط ب ج د).
ḥa is not a qalqalah letter.
kha is not a qalqalah letter.
jim is a qalqalah letter.

questions.q: Which English sound is closest to خ?
explain: Right: a light scrape near the top of the throat.
'k' stops completely; خ keeps flowing.
'h' has no scrape; it is closer to ه.
That is jim.

questions.q: Persian and Urdu readers often say ح like which letter?
explain: Right: in Persian and Urdu both are a plain 'h', so they merge.
kha scrapes; the usual merge is with the plain 'h' of ه.
ʿayn is a voiced throat letter; the usual merge is with ه.
jim is made with the tongue, not the throat.
Right: ḥa is the hook alone.
jim has one dot below.
kha has one dot above.
nun has one dot above.

questions.q: In the middle of a word, what tells ج, ح and خ apart?
options: The dot: below, none or above
Whether it joins the next letter
explain: Right: the hook looks the same; only the dot differs.
The tail appears only at the end of a word or standing alone.
Colours show tajweed rules, not letters.
All three join the next letter.

options: The part of the throat nearest the mouth
The deepest part of the throat
explain: Right: kha and ghayn come from the part of the throat nearest the mouth.
That is ḥa and ʿayn.
That is hamza and ha (ه).
That is jim, shin and ya.

options: The part of the throat nearest the mouth
explain: Right: jim, shin and ya come from the middle of the tongue.
That is ḥa and ʿayn.
That is ba, mim and waw.
That is kha and ghayn.

questions.q: Your ح has a scrape in it, like خ. What fixes it?
options: Bring it down to the middle of the throat and let the breath flow smoothly
Raise the back of the tongue higher
explain: Right: ḥa is a smooth, squeezed breath with no scrape.
Raising the tongue makes it heavier, more like kha.
Voice and a gargle push it towards ghayn.
The lips are not used for ḥa.

questions.q: Which TWO letters of this family are whispered (the breath keeps flowing)?
explain: Right: both are in the whispered (hams) group.
jim holds its breath back (jahr); only ḥa of these two is whispered.
jim holds its breath back; only kha of these two is whispered.
jim is not whispered.

questions.q: How should ج sound in recitation?
explain: Right: the tongue presses, holds, then releases cleanly.
'zh' keeps flowing; jim is a strong letter that stops.
'g' is made further back in the mouth; it is not jim.
'y' is the letter ي.

remnote: ج (jim) == Dot below; middle of the tongue; firm 'j' as in 'jam'; light; bounces with sukun
ح (ḥa) == No dot; middle of the throat; smooth whispered breath, no scrape; light
خ (kha) == Dot above; part of the throat nearest the mouth; 'ch' in 'loch'; heavy
Persian/Urdu fix for ح == Squeeze the middle of the throat so it does not become ه
